Check out these stories: I’m Gojko Adzic, author of Running Serverless, Impact Mapping, Humans vs Computers, and a few more books. My book Specification by Example won the Jolt Award for the best book of 2012. I’m one of the 2019 AWS Serverless Heroes, the winner of the 2016 European Software Testing Outstanding Achievement Award, and the 2011 Most Influential Agile Testing Professional Award. I’m the founder of Naraket and one of the co-founders of MindMup. Narakeet is an online service that helps people make narrated videos easily. It is a text-to-speech video maker, aimed at people who are not video professionals, such as developers, online educators, and marketers. In brief, it turns PowerPoint presentations and markdown files into videos, creating life-like narration from speaker notes and voice-over scripts. Users can edit video as simply as they would edit text, saving hours by not having to record and re-record audio, synchronize pictures with sound and transcribe subtitles. The product was launched in public beta in April 2020, and commercially in October 2020. Roughly 80K users created 220,000 videos since the launch. Narakeet now supports 40+ languages and local accents, with more than 250 high-quality neural engine voices. Neural-network AI voices are so good now that they can sound better than people who are not native speakers of the target language, or even native speakers with a strong accent. Text-to-speech narration is also amazing for people who need to record a voice-over but do not have professional audio equipment or a sound-proof environment, or are not pro voiceover artists. Narakeet helps to make videos faster by automating most of the voiceover and editing. What s your backstory and how did you get into entrepreneurship? I’ve been fascinated with programming since early childhood. Making products with software is the closest thing to magic today. Like wizards from folk tales, we turn some cryptic words into stuff that people can interact with in real life. Plant the seed somewhere, then see how it takes root, then water it with lots of attention and user feedback. Growing products like that are very satisfying. I started by copying PEEK/POKE instructions from Commodore 64 magazines as a kid in the eighties, making the computer wake up my folks with weird sounds. In high school, I competed in demoscene assembly programming, and then halfway through university realized that I can make money doing stuff I loved. I went through a bunch of programming jobs in the late nineties and early 00s then started working for myself. I created a consultancy business that helps large organizations, mostly financial institutions, improve software delivery (It’s still going strong, although these days my partners have taken over most client engagements.) Somewhere along that journey I ended up realizing that the kinds of jobs I was working were not fun anymore. The money was great, but the fun was gone. Then I started building my products and rediscovered the joy of programming. In 2013 I co-founded MindMup, an app that millions of students and schoolchildren use to capture ideas, structure writing assignments, and organize thoughts. In 2020, I launched Narakeet. In the meantime, I also co-founded and built a bunch of stuff that didn’t do that well, including a social games platform, a post-conference engagement app for event organizers, a developer-oriented testing tool, and a video game about what would happen if East Germany survived till today and Stasi ran Google and Facebook. Most of my businesses were bootstrapped, funded initially by my consulting work or other stuff I built. Take us through your entrepreneurial journey. How did you go from day 1 to today? In addition to all this other stuff, I also like making open-source products. One was Claudia.js, an open-source tool for deploying Lambda functions to AWS. Claudia was one of the early tools that tried to make the process straightforward while AWS was still getting its act together around serverless. The key thing there was developer experience, and I wanted to make video tutorials for Claudia so that people could get started easily. Coming up with the video content was easy and fun. The rest of the experience was frustrating. Aligning pictures and synchronizing them with sound felt like a huge waste of time. Recording narration was even worse. It took me seven attempts to do a single paragraph without mistakes. It still sounded bad, so I gave up and paid a professional voice artist. Her voice was great, but she spoke slower than me, so I had to re-edit the videos again. For one video, it took me more than four hours of effort to create just five minutes of good content. Six months later, a web page is shown in that tutorial significantly changed, and I wanted to update it. Instead of a simple tweak, it all came crashing down. I foolishly tried to save money by asking the artist to record just the changed part. It was the same person, the same equipment, but you could hear the difference. I had to choose between a video that sounded inconsistent, or paying for the whole thing again and wasting time on re-editing everything. There had to be a better way of making videos, but I couldn’t find any, so I decided to build it. It all started with a bunch of shell scripts, and soon it was taking me ten to fifteen minutes to make a great five-minute video, not hours like before. Around the time the video workflow came together, YCombinator decided to open up its Startup School program to a remote audience. I wanted to participate but needed a product to take from the idea to launch in a few months. I thought that other people who are not video professionals must have the same problems I had and that it would be fun to try turning my shell scripts into a product so others can benefit as well. That’s how Narakeet came to be. Narakeet takes care of all the boring and time-consuming tasks of video editing, and lets users focus on creating good content. It will automatically create video clips from images, align audio and video segments, add captions, display text on top of videos and apply transitions between scenes. It will record life-like narration using neural text-to-speech systems, so the audio will be consistent no matter how many times you change the script. The tool was originally intended for techies like me, who like to script stuff. Having videos built from text, with support for version control, continuous integration, and building pipelines is very liberating for people like that (it even supports GitHub actions so you can rebuild videos automatically when your screenshots change). The tool found its way to a much wider audience that has the same problem, but can’t use any markdown, GitHub, or even cares about continuous integration. This crazy covid pandemic made video lessons more important than ever before, and teachers all of the sudden had to become good at video editing. They rarely have the skills or the equipment to make good videos, let alone the time. (One NCTQ study found that teachers can afford to spend, on average, about 45 minutes a day planning lessons.) A bunch of teaching sites started recommending my tool and I discovered that there’s a much wider market for it than I originally thought. After a lot of user research, an idea emerged to just let people convert slides into videos. Teachers already prepared lectures in Powerpoint or something similar, and they’d usually type up the stuff they wanted to speak about in presenter notes. Narakeet just took that idea and did the next logical step. It turns slides into a video by using the presenter s notes for voice-over. title: Korea Advances Physical AI Across Industries With NVIDIA
summary: Tapping into the country’s strengths in manufacturing and engineering, NVIDIA is helping advance Korea’s physical AI ecosystem. The country’s industry leaders are applying accelerated computing, AI and simulation to everything from semiconductor manufacturing to robotics and autonomous vehicles. These efforts are helping bring physical AI from development into real-world production. Samsung Advances Semiconductor Engineering With Accelerated Computing and AI Physics Samsung Electronics is expanding its collaboration with NVIDIA to advance semiconductor innovation through accelerated computing and AI physics. The work spans materials research, process development and device engineering. title: Korea’s AI Ecosystem Advances and Secures Agentic AI With NVIDIA
summary: As AI agents take on more work, they need capable open models and security that advances alongside them. Hyundai Motor Group is exploring NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprints and the NVIDIA OpenShell runtime, while AIM Intelligence is integrating its Starfort platform with NVIDIA OpenShell to support secure AI agents for employee productivity and enterprise workflows . A key component of the NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform, OpenShell provides a secure runtime with sandboxed execution and policy-based controls to safeguard sensitive data, manage access to enterprise tools and govern autonomous agent actions. AIM Intelligence , a Korean AI security company, is integrating its Starfort agent control platform with NVIDIA OpenShell. title: From Chips to Skills, NVIDIA and Korea Expand Sovereign AI Collaboration
summary: NVIDIA and Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT) are expanding their collaboration across the country’s sovereign AI ecosystem, from AI semiconductors and data center infrastructure to talent, startups, models, agents and security. The collaboration lays the groundwork for Korean NPU and XPU companies to explore participation in the NVIDIA NVLink Fusion ecosystem, and includes NVIDIA training and certification programs, hackathons and technical seminars to strengthen GPU utilization. Read more in the press release .

title: NVIDIA Dynamo Recipes Bring Korea’s Leading Open Models to Production
summary: NVIDIA is releasing Dynamo-optimized deployment recipes for Korea’s leading open models: A.X K2 from SK Telecom , K-EXAONE 2.0 from LG AI Research , Solar Open 2 from Upstage and Motif-3 from Motif Technologies . As models grow beyond the capacity of a single GPU, they must be split across multiple GPUs, requiring careful coordination of request routing and communication to maintain performance. NVIDIA Dynamo is an open source, distributed inference-serving framework built to deploy models in multi-node environments at data center scale. It handles this routing and communication to maximize inference performance. Optimized for NVIDIA B200 GPUs, these recipes take the guesswork out of deployment, delivering up to 2x performance out of the box. They help developers bring Korea’s open models into production faster and turn them into broadly accessible AI for All services. Learn more about NVIDIA Dynamo .

title: 一颗植物工厂草莓，离你的果盘还有多远？多多农研拉近现场
summary: 作者｜徐珊 编辑｜ 郑玄 这可能是你见过最安静的一块「草莓地」。 没有虫鸣，没有鸟叫，50 平方米的房间里，草莓植株一层层码到头顶，叶片舒展，几乎找不到一个虫眼，枝头挂满了还没转红的青果，也有不少已经熟透。不靠天、不靠地，草莓在这个赛博农场里被「种上了天」。 这里是第五届「多多农研科技大赛」一等奖赛博农人团队的植物工厂。从 5 月 12 日定植算起，这些草莓等了 113 天才迎来第一次采收，采收 50 天累计产量达到 284.45 公斤，而日常照料它们的，只有 1 名工人。评委贺冬仙说，如果再给它半年，这一架草莓产量会相当可观。 但每一束光、每一度低温背后都是成本。过去几年，Plenty、Bowery、Infarm 等明星垂直农业公司相继破产或停运。到 2024 年，中国已经有了 493 座植物工厂，研究机构、照明企业等都在入场，但其中不少也处于亏损状态。 植物工厂离商业化，始终只差临门一脚。 种出植物并不是结果，过去几年，植物工厂的技术一直在进步，但成本的账却始终算不平。这两年，前沿技术更深地介入种植，光配方、环控算法和立体栽培，迭代明显提速。据大赛评委、中国农业大学水利与土木工程学院教授贺冬仙估算，按一等奖获得者赛博农人团队的势头，如果全年持续生产，每平方米能产出 8 公斤草莓，可以追平全日本一季植物工厂草莓的最高单产水平。 正因为有 50 平方米、国产设备、有限经费、选手不能进厂、操作工是新人等这些约束，植物工厂最真实的难处才被逼了出来。软硬件到底好不好，都得由植物来判断。 国产植物工厂方案离商业化还差什么？当工程师的算法遇上老农的经验，未来的农业会发生什么变化？ 这也是拼多多连续五年办这场比赛的用意，从帮农民把农产品卖出去，走到用技术帮农民把地种好。在商业化的前夜，它更像一次互相校准 。 01 九死一生的垂直农业， 为什么最后都押注了草莓？ 如果把过去几年倒下的垂直农业公司列一张名单，会发现一个奇怪的规律，只要是种生菜的几乎全军覆没，活下来的都只种一种植物：草莓。 仅 2025 年一年，室内农业相关的破产就有 14 起。以种叶菜为主的 Bowery 停运，Infarm 裁掉近一半员工、退出欧洲；背靠软银、沃尔玛和贝索斯的 Plenty 破产重组后，砍掉了所有业务，只留下一座草莓工厂。为什么草莓得到了大家的如此偏好？既然大家都押注草莓，为什么全世界至今还没有一座草莓植物工厂，能单靠卖草莓收支持平？ 其实，早在 6 年前，第一届「多多农研科技大赛」种的就是草莓。几支 AI 赛道队伍在云南富民的高原温室里远程操控，和当地农人同台比拼，平均产量比传统农人高出 196%，只是甜度还输了一截。后来，比赛先后换成樱桃番茄和生菜，甚至干脆拿掉土壤和阳光，把赛场搬进植物工厂；上一届，选手们还要在预算之内亲手把集装箱改造成植物工厂。 比赛现场种植出的草莓，口感软滑 | 来源：极客公园 时隔三届，为什么今年又种回了草莓？ 中国农业科学院都市农业研究所首席科学家杨其长提到，这其实离不开草莓的特殊性。 简单来说，就是，比草莓好种的没草莓值钱，比草莓值钱的没草莓好种。 叶菜生长周期短、适合人工光，早期植物工厂几乎都在种叶菜，但它的溢价很难比露天和温室种出来的高太多。 草莓如果在露天和温室种植，其产季主要集中在 12 月到次年 4 月，其他的时间基本无法种植。因为草莓必须经历夜温低于 12 度的花芽分化，在热带，它甚至根本种不出来。如果遇到天灾或者气候不给力，草莓也很难长好，完全靠天吃饭。但环境控制，恰恰是植物工厂最有优势的地方。 中国农业科学院都市农业研究所首席科学家杨其长 但这也意味着，草莓的溢价几乎全部来自「错季」。在市场空窗期，植物工厂的草莓可以靠价格撑起成本；一到草莓季，它就很难和大棚草莓拼价格，更别说全年不停的水电和运营开支。海外的幸存者靠卖高端草莓站住了市场，Oishii 起家时一盒卖到 50 美元，但这很难成为普通人的日常。且不同市场的草莓用途也不一样，欧美的草莓更多做成果酱和甜品，产量高就行；中国、日本、韩国的消费者买的是鲜食，看重的是口感。 贺冬仙则坦言，眼下还没有一座工厂能证明草莓植物工厂可以靠卖草莓回本，「但这并不能说明未来三五年之内不能出现」。这一届比赛瞄准的，正是这道商业化的题。50 平方米、有限的经费、国产设备、没有经验的操作工，还要同时兼顾品质、能耗和成本。 在这样的条件下，他们会给出什么样的中国解法？ 02 170 天，一群工程师被草莓「上了一课」 「最终还是要用植物来检验。」贺冬仙说。这句话几乎贯穿了整场比赛，无论是老专家还是领域新手，最后都被一颗草莓上了一课。 考验来得比想象中更早，最早甚至能追溯到种苗上。5 月正值种苗淡季，为了省钱，拟生态团队从浙江建德的地里运来一批苗，进厂前做过处理，看上去干干净净，但没灭菌先闹蚜虫，后起了白粉病。隔壁欧普智莓的工厂里，AI 在 5 月中旬识别出叶螨，也是因为种苗问题，一个月后，类似炭疽病的真菌蔓延开来，这支用电最省的队伍收成却不理想。 拟生态团队搭建的 50 平方米比赛场地一角 | 来源：极客公园 可苗的问题，远不止干不干净。比苗更早决定一座工厂上限的，是种什么品种。 中国是全球最大的草莓生产国，种的却长期是进口草莓品种。日本的「红颜」在中国的种植面积，是日本本土的 8 倍多。草莓品种权一直被国外拿住话语权。这一届比赛要求全程种植国产品种，粉玉、越王、越秀轮番登场。但这些品种原本是为大田和温室选育的，搬进植物工厂后会有什么表现，参赛队员心里并没有底。 即便育种人亲自参与种植，也在室温与根系温度之间，失了判断。 除了种苗，第二个让选手们栽了跟头的因素，竟然是人。 在植物工厂里，一切都是可控的，灯、温度、水分、肥料，唯一不可控的是操作工，这样让人的一举一动，影响更大。 按照比赛规则，选手不能进厂，170 天里的日常照料全部交给工人，而他们大多不是专业的种植人员。有些操作，工人未必理解背后的用意，选手又只能靠工人的汇报判断情况。「你问他每天长怎么样，他说不明白，有可能就拍一两个地方看看。」莓立方的队员说，不少镜头以外的问题就这样被漏了过去，等发现时已经晚了。赛博农人也承认一开始「缺乏考虑工人作业因素」，指令下得不够细，执行回来总有偏差，好在他们发现得早，补得也快。照明、空调、灌溉都可以交给系统，唯独对草莓长势的判断最难交出去。它涉及植物本身的生理，「有一定随机性和未知性」，至今仍离不开资深师傅的眼睛。 还有一些因素，连人都很难理解。 莓立方的近百只熊蜂进厂后集体「罢工」，不出巢、啃花，甚至攻击人，排查到最后才发现，蜂箱被摆在了噪音和气流扰动最大的地方，熊蜂应激了。熊蜂还是红色盲，植物工厂常用的红光、白光恰好让它看不清花，拟生态团队只好在灯里加入紫光，给熊蜂「指路」。 在植物工厂里，就连一只蜂的感受和视线，也得被考虑清楚。其实我们看到 AI 越来越会种地的时代，人的价值反而变得更清晰了。工程师则要学会让不懂植物的人也能看懂草莓的情绪，专家是把几十年经验翻译教会算法，工人是工厂里最后的眼睛和手。 03 「懂植物的工程师和懂技术的农民该站一起」 工程的力量，在于把过去非标准的东西标准化。种草莓靠经验、靠手感，是农业里最难标准化的事情之一，而这一届比赛逼着选手们把它拆成一项项可以计算的技术。每一个技术方案，最后都得考虑清楚每一度电、每一滴水应该如何被消耗。 光是植物工厂里最大的一笔电费，也是最好的调味剂。赛博农人的工厂里，光占了总能耗的近一半。他们自研的白红 LED 灯具，把红光和蓝光按 2.9 比 1 调配，在不减产的前提下提高了草莓的甜度，系统还会根据冠层图像判断植株所处的阶段，随时调整灯光。拟生态的灯装得比别支队伍多出 20 千瓦，供电却撑不住，一组灯始终没能打开，成为赛事遗憾之一。 但除了光，节水也是降本的方式之一。赛博农人团队连空调除湿时冷凝下来的水也没浪费，回收率超过 75%，又被送回去浇了草莓，绝不浪费任何一点资源。 莓立方团队的种植架每层均配备独立风扇，构建高效的内部空气循环系统 在植物工厂里，空间的上限最终由均匀度决定。空间上，四支队伍拿到的都是同样的占地 50 平方米的植物工厂，但思路却各不相同。他们不约而同都选择轨道移动栽培架，几排架子平时间隔开来，待工人作业时可适当收缩留出一条通道，赛博农人由此把种植面积拓展至了 126 平方米；莓立方更在意每一层能不能活得一样好，用中央风道把 110 根细风道送到冠层，给每株草莓配了一个「专属呼吸孔」，栽培架上下层温差压在 0.5 度以内；拟生态则押注密度、冲刺产量，种下 4400 余株，事后才发现在环境控制要求下，这座工厂承载量有限，灯开不全，光照不够，草莓越长越小。 此次比赛一等奖获得者赛博农人团队 | 来源：极客公园 但真正握住这些钥匙的，是工厂的「大脑」。过去是人给植物设定环境，现在是植物的需求在驱动环境。赛博农人把自己的大脑运作逻辑叫作「与植物对话」：先把专家经验和文献知识写进一张草莓全生育期的知识图谱，作为环境参数的起点；再把整座工厂当成一片巨大的叶子，连续监测里面的二氧化碳交换和蒸腾，读懂这群草莓此刻是在呼吸还是在光合。 莓立方则给草莓建了一个数字模型，让算法先「模拟种植」，现实再照着执行，技术的力量正在逐渐渗透到各个环节。 可这个大脑还没有完全长成，吕兆晨说，团队里的专家看一眼叶片边缘的焦黄，三秒钟就知道是缺水还是缺光，「我们可以把其中一个环节写成代码，但那三秒的整体感，我至今不知道怎么建模」。「未来农业不是不需要农民，而是需要懂植物的工程师和懂技术的农民站一起。」吕兆晨说道。 04 在农研的慢赛道上， 拼多多搭起一座「练兵场」 「参加比赛之前，我一直以为做农业的人不多，与我同龄的人更少。」一位莓立方的队员说。在上海交大，做农业的人本就不多，愿意做植物工厂的更少，这是一个小众领域里更小众的方向。可在这场比赛里，这位队员遇到了赛博农人那群年纪相仿的同行，也看到育种专家、企业工程师从完全不同的角度去琢磨一颗草莓的长势。「我们不是一个很庞大的群体，但至少还有同龄人。能在植物工厂这条路上有结伴同行的人，对我来说非常重要。」 这条路需要更多人，也需要技术持续跟进。比赛结束了，植物工厂的故事还在继续。拟生态团队的浅液流方案已经在新加坡一所大学里运行了一年多，莓立方团队正在推动把自己的工厂搬进交大校园做教学基地，上一届的墨泉团队则早早把植物工厂运到了西藏亚东，让近十年才吃上叶菜的当地居民，吃上了家门口种出来的新鲜蔬菜 拟生态团队采用浅液流栽培方案，仅用约 40 天就收获头茬草莓| 来源：极客公园 对拼多多来说，这场比赛也不只是一次科研投入。拼多多从农产品电商起家，农业是它的起家之本，也是它这些年始终投入的方向。2025 年拼多多推出「千亿扶持」计划，不断加码农业科技投入，多多农研科技大赛正是其中的重要抓手。 在拼多多看来，助农不只是帮农民把农产品卖出去，更要用技术破解农业的难题。比赛把题目设在真实的生产环境里，让高校、企业和育种专家同场试错，再用大众评审把结果交给消费者检验。这是一件「难而正确」的事，也是一家从农业里长出来的公司，回过头来为农业做的长期功课。 大众评审员对大赛收获的草莓进行感官评价 一颗草莓背后，是一场更大的农业变革。截至 2024 年，全国现代设施种植面积已经达到 4000 万亩；2025 年，农产品网络零售额达到 7833 亿元，越来越多的果蔬通过手机下单、直达餐桌。消费者要的不只是买得到，更是品质稳定、四季都有，这些期待，最终都要靠田间地头的技术一点点兑现。植物工厂里攻下的光配方、环控算法和种植经验，也不会只留在 50 平方米的赛博农场里。 「农业是一个慢赛道。」欧普智莓的队员提到，它需要时间沉淀，需要大量真实的数据，也需要一次次复盘和迭代。当一拨人向着具身智能、飞行汽车全速奔跑时，另一拨人把 AI 技术用在了离土地最近的地方，在一座安静的草莓工厂里，跟温度、熊蜂和电费较劲了 170 天。前沿科技决定我们能走多远，而这样一群有创新思维的青年人，决定未来科技能不能真正落回生活，影响我们每一个人。 *头图来源：极客公园 title: 实测 HY4：腾讯最「夯」大模型，离一线还有多远？
summary: 头图来源：腾讯混元 11 月 4 日，混元 Hy4 正式发布，模型权重将在近期开源，主打性价比的轻量版 Hy4 flash 也一起亮相。腾讯给它的定位是——首次跻身最强开源模型之列。 过去一年，腾讯在 AI 上最多被人看见的，是 WorkBuddy 这类 Agent 和应用产品；到了更底层的模型上，它的声量明显弱于应用。Hy4 真正要回答的，是腾讯在模型这条线上的身位。 从榜单表现来看，在开源模型里，Hy4 已经站进第一梯队；放到全球，和顶尖闭源模型的差距仍然清晰。 而根据国家数据局最近公布的一组数据，我国日均 Token 调用量已经从 2024 年初的 1000 亿，增长到今年 7 月的超 500 万亿，两年增长超 5000 倍。Token 消耗狂飙的背后，Agent 正在从一个技术概念变成新的生产力形态。 极客公园围绕长程 Agent、多模态理解与视觉代码等主线，结合官方评测数据和典型任务，进行了实测，以梳理这一代 Hy4 到底补上了哪些能力。 一、长程 Agent：门槛在「把一整件事跑完」 过去测模型，行业习惯看单轮问答、单道题目的表现。进入 Agent 阶段，变成看跨多轮、跨多步、长时间运行，模型能不能始终记得目标在哪里、自己能走到哪一步，中途出错能不能自己拉回来，最后形成逻辑闭环的交付。 最近对 CPO 赛道关注比较多，我给 Hy4 安排了一个接近买方真实工作的任务： 让它扮演覆盖 AI 算力产业链的研究员，围绕 CPO（共封装光学）赛道，做一份面向投资决策委员会的深度研究报告和可复算估值模型，数据截至最近一个已完成的交易日。 2026 年被称为 CPO 量产元年，英伟达 Spectrum-X、博通 Bailly 等 CPO 交换机陆续进入客户导入，台积电 COUPE 投产、谷歌 NPO 订单落地，产业事件密集；与此同时，A 股光通信「易中天」（中际旭创、新易盛、天孚通信）以及光芯片、光器件公司的股价和估值已经大幅抬升。投委会真正想知道的，是这条链当前还能不能配、该怎么配。 任务要求几乎覆盖了一名研究员的完整工作流。它先要梳理 CPO 产业链图谱——上游光芯片、激光器、硅光、光器件，中游光引擎、光模块，下游交换机和云厂商——并配一张可视化产业链图；同时讲清 CPO 与传统可插拔光模块、NPO、OOI 的技术差异、替代节奏和关键催化节点，引用英伟达、博通、台积电的官方路线图和时间点。 视频来源：极客公园 数据核验是这道题最容易露馅的环节。模型需要获取重点公司近 3 年财报、最新行情与市值、业务结构、毛利率和机构一致预期，还要兼顾英伟达、博通、Coherent、Lumentum 等海外映射数据；每个数字都要标明来源、日期、币种和单位，区分实际值、预测值和假设，缺失数据明确说明，禁止编造数据、机构或分析师身份。我们还特别要求它核实各家公司是否真正进入海外巨头 CPO 供应链，严格区分已量产、送样测试和仅披露合作意向三种状态，把「蹭概念」的标的识别出来。 在此基础上，它要从 A 股选 4 家覆盖光模块、光器件、光芯片环节的代表公司做横向对比表，并测算当前估值隐含的增长预期，结合一致预期判断预期差在哪里，给出乐观、基准、悲观三情景；再选一家最看好的公司建立可复算的未来三年利润表模型，关键假设集中管理，验证勾稽关系，禁止无解释倒挤。最后，它还得正面回答投委会三问：当前是业绩兑现还是主题炒作，哪个环节弹性最大，如果只能选一家该选谁。 从实际运行看，Hy4 沿用了它处理长任务的典型路径：先拆解任务、列出执行计划，再分阶段推进，中间做阶段性自检。产业链图谱、技术路线、对比表和三情景能够依次落地，数据来源、假设口径和不确定性都有明确标注，模型内的勾稽关系可以对上，最终交付的是报告 PDF 加估值模型 xls。 官方金融众测数据可以作为参照，腾讯基于真实金融场景构建了数千个工作空间和上万个高质量任务，覆盖基金研究、证券分析、量化策略、资产配置和财税会计等流程，并联合腾讯金融科技 FiT 组织了 213 位专家参与众测，其中 153 位来自外部头部金融机构，七成拥有五年以上工作经验。在 579 个真实金融任务上，Hy4 拿到 3.04 分，在开源模型中排名第一，高于 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 的 2.97、Kimi K3.1 Pro 和 GLM-5.3 的 2.68；在金融智能体公司讯兔科技的内部评测 IRAB 中，Hy4 较 preview 版提升 12.03 个百分点。 更基础的一项改进在事实准确性。针对时效检索、多源信息整合和事实一致性，混元做了专项搜索优化，Hy4 的幻觉率从 preview 版的 12.95% 降到 7.2%，猜测导致的错误率从 23.1% 大幅降到 5.6%。对需要引用大量数据和资料的研究任务来说，这两个数字的意义，比任何跑分都直接。 长程能力的差距，往往就藏在最后一公里。前面九成的步骤，今天第一梯队的模型大多能做，能不能把文件真的生成出来、数字对得上、打开就能用，才是分水岭。Hy4 在这一环的表现，具备了「初级研究助理」的雏形。 当然，这类任务依然离不开人来验收。模型会标注数据口径、假设合理性和最终结论，但投委会上的决策责任，依旧没有任何模型能替研究员承担。 二、视觉理解与视觉代码：混元第一次长出「眼睛」 Hy4 这一代最值得关注的变化，是首次引入视觉理解。混元此前走的是纯语言模型路线，这一代开始能够看懂图像、图表、截图和视频，并把视觉信息转化为输出。按照官方说法，它已经能完成细粒度图像处理、复杂图表分析和数学视觉推理这三类任务。 我们把测试重心放在了依赖视觉还原的代码任务上，这也是多模态能力最容易见真章的地方。第一个任务是一个交互式 3D 机械腕表机芯拆解网页。 要求用 Three.js 展示一枚程序化建模的机械腕表，至少包含表壳、表圈、表镜、表盘、时针分针秒针、齿轮系（至少 3 个相互啮合的齿轮）、发条盒、摆轮、机芯底板和表冠，全部用程序化几何体实现；支持旋转、缩放、拆解和复原，点击零件要高亮并显示名称、作用和简短说明；拆解动画要按照「表壳表圈表镜 → 表盘指针 → 齿轮系 → 摆轮与发条盒 → 机芯底板」的顺序展开，各部件保持原有空间对应关系，不能随机散开；还要有一套机芯运转演示，摆轮持续往复摆动、齿轮按啮合关系联动、指针同步走时，动画可重复播放；最终交付可运行工程，并确认控制台没有阻断性报错。 视频来源：极客公园 生成这样一个网页，模型要先用程序化几何体把十几个零件逐一搭出来，给每个零件挂好层级和坐标，拆解时按顺序移动、保证彼此位置不错位，再让齿轮和摆轮持续运转。按照官方评测和任务要求，它能够把旋转、缩放、拆解、复原整套交互跑通，点击零件会弹出说明，控制台没有报错。 第二个任务是让它复刻开发一个游戏《NAIAD 水泽仙女》的网页版同款，需要和视频里的游戏玩法相似。 复刻版《NAIAD 水泽仙女》｜视频来源：极客公园 制作过程｜视频来源：极客公园 可以看到，在这轮实测里，Hy4 其实是把视频取证、机制抽象和渲染回读串成了一个闭环：先用 ffmpeg 把 81 秒录屏抽帧、拼图、局部放大，反复辨认出「白色人鱼游动、收集光点、碰花苞绽放、穿石环泛光晕、章节卡淡入、无分数无死亡」这套玩法，再用单文件 Canvas 2D 手写重实现一遍。关键不在「照着画面还原」——配色、花瓣、光晕都是按氛围重新画的，还原的是机制而非像素。 真正让成品收敛的其实是后半圈，用无头浏览器真跑、截图、再把截图读回来比对，连续揪出宽屏花丛被裁、转屏坐标错位、光点收不满、章节门槛卡死四个问题，改完再跑，循环四五轮直到章节推进和按钮全部通过。这是一条「多帧看懂 → 重做一遍 → 渲染回读验证」的回路：视觉理解只负责给方向，把主观判断变成可验证事实的，则是回头自检。 此外，电脑操作是 Hy4 首次支持的能力。它能像人一样看懂屏幕，再用鼠标键盘操作浏览器、桌面应用和操作系统，命令行与图形界面都能用；针对 Blender、CAD 等专业软件和跨应用长任务，混元还做了专项训练。 三、从「能聊」到「能交」，混元只是把拼图补齐了 上面测试线放在一起看，可以看到腾讯没有把主要精力压在单榜跑分上，而是让模型在真实业务场景里持续进化。 今年 2 月重建基础设施以来，混元平均每两个月推出一个大版本，先以 Preview 开放、再根据反馈发布正式版。8 月的 Hy4 preview 总参数 770 亿、激活参数 490 亿、支持近百万 token 输入，定位「为生产力而生」，上线后长期位于 OpenRouter 排行前列；这一代 Hy4 补上的，是长程闭环、视觉理解和电脑操作这几块关键拼图。 在开源阵营，除了 Agent Arena

title: 黄仁勋承认「婚外情」，英伟达启动调查；ChatGPT 突现封号风波，200 美元 Pro 用户也遭殃；腾讯姚顺雨谈「AI 公司护城河」：在产品层，而不是模型层
summary: 黄仁勋承认「婚外情」，英伟达启动调查 11 月 9 日消息，英伟达 CEO 黄仁勋当地时间 8 日于公司官网发布致全员公开信，就个人私事致歉，同时披露董事会将针对相关报道提及的国家安全关切展开独立调查。 黄仁勋在信中承认自己对妻子不忠，坦言该行为伤害家人，对此承担全部责任，并接受外界批评。他表示家人不应为其个人选择负责，恳请公众给予家人隐私空间，希望能有机会重新赢回家人信任。他强调自己对英伟达始终坚定，将努力重新赢得团队与投资方的信赖。 针对近期报道带出的国家安全相关质疑，黄仁勋确认董事会已启动独立调查，本人将全力配合。 此前据《纽约时报》报道，美国政府认为黄仁勋与一家名为 Megaspeed 的新加坡科技公司前高管 Alice Huang（黄乐）存在密切关系。（来源：DoNews） 特斯拉更新 AI 加速器路线图：SI6 算力达 HW4 的 80 倍，Dojo D3 将面向太空部署 11 月 8 日消息，特斯拉公布了更新后的 AI 加速器路线图，进一步揭示了公司未来几年的芯片研发方向。根据这份路线图，特斯拉第六代推理加速器的算力预计将达到现有第四代芯片的 80 倍；而用于训练任务的 Dojo D3 将放弃以 SRAM 为核心的架构，转向采用多芯粒设计，并搭载堆叠式 HBM 高带宽内存。 此外，特斯拉还开始用「超级智能」（Super Intelligence，SI）取代「人工智能」（Artificial Intelligence，AI）这一名称，为旗下 AI 加速器启用 SI 系列命名。出于相同原因，马斯克近期也确认，SpaceXAI 将更名为 SpaceXSI。 这份路线图中最值得关注的变化，或许是特斯拉重新启动了自主研发的 Dojo 训练加速器项目。 马斯克曾在 2025 年 8 月取消整个晶圆级 Dojo 项目，并于 2026 年 8 月表示，SpaceX 和 xAI 将在其地面及太空数据中心中全部采用英伟达硬件。不过，第三代 Dojo D3 与前两代 Dojo D1、Dojo D2 将有明显不同。 特斯拉将下一代 Dojo D3 描述为一款基于芯粒（Chiplet）的训练加速器，采用 2.5D 和 3D 封装技术，并搭载堆叠式 HBM 内存。（来源：IT 之家） 亚马逊成立新团队专攻家用机器人，剑指「前所未有」的新产品 11 月 8 日消息，分析亚马逊的招聘信息发现，过去几个月，亚马逊组建了一支新团队，准备开发 一款前 所未有的机器人产品。 亚马逊近期发布的一则工程师招聘信息写道：「机器人即将走出电影，进入我们的家中。」这条被撤掉的招聘信息透露，新产品能够适应不断变化的家庭环境，并在人类家庭成员身边自主活动。 亚马逊一向愿意押注长期项目，即便短期内不被外界理解，只要能够帮助公司抢占新市场的先机，就值得投入。此前的 Alexa 语音助手和 Kindle 电子书阅读器，都采用了这种发展策略。 亚马逊 CEO 安迪 · 贾西在最近的年度股东信中重申了这一思路，认为人工智能和机器人技术将带来人们一生中最重大的变革之一。「我们努力预判什么能让客户每天的生活更轻松、更美好，并创造下一个重大转折点。」 LinkedIn 个人资料显示，今年早些时候，亚马逊将 Astro 项目的大部分成员调往其他岗位，还聘请了一名麻省理工学院的机器人专家参与家用机器人研发。 至于新团队究竟打算开发什么样的家用机器人、能让机器人完成哪些任务，目前还没有明确消息。不过，亚马逊 6 月的一则招聘信息透露，研发目标不仅是让机器人具备实用功能，还要让用户在使用过程中感到愉悦。（来源：IT 之家） 苹果 Siri AI 团队或迎大调整，工程副总裁罗克韦尔考虑明年走人 11 月 8 日消息，马克 · 古尔曼在刚更新的《Power On》时事通讯中爆料，曾主导 Vision Pro 头显开发、同时负责新版 Siri AI 项目的迈克 · 罗克韦尔，仍在认真考虑离开现有岗位。 古尔曼披露，罗克韦尔或将于明年卸任 Siri 工程副总裁，甚至彻底离开苹果。新版 Siri 跳票了两年才得以上市，考虑到罗克韦尔在其中发挥的作用，他的离开将给苹果造成重大损失。 如果罗克韦尔最终离职，或在苹果内部转任其他岗位，更多工作预计将交给两名高管：去年从谷歌加入苹果、负责加强 AI 业务的阿马尔 · 苏布拉马尼亚，以及费德里吉的副手塞巴斯蒂安 · 马里诺。 苹果内部一些人认为，马里诺未来有望接替费德里吉出任软件工程主管，而且他对 AI 发展的态度更加积极。据悉，马里诺负责的团队主要承担将 AI 技术整合到 iOS 系统中的工作。（来源：IT 之家） ChatGPT 突现封号风波，200 美元 Pro 用户也遭殃 近日，多名用户在 Reddit 及 OpenAI 官方开发者社区反映，自己的 ChatGPT 账号突然遭到停用，其中包括每月订阅费用为 200 美元的 Pro 用户。部分用户表示，账号被封前没有收到任何通知，长期积累的聊天记录和工作资料也因此无法访问。 11 月 7 日，一名用户在 OpenAI 官方开发者社区发帖称，自己的 ChatGPT Pro 账号当天突然被停用，系统显示错误代码「account_deactivated」，但没有收到任何预警或封禁通知邮件。 该用户表示，自己不仅是 ChatGPT Pro 订阅用户，还加入了 OpenAI 的网络安全相关访问计划，账号启用了需要实体安全密钥验证的高级安全设置。他怀疑，封号可能与自己近期通过不同地区的 VPN 节点访问 ChatGPT 和 Codex 有关。不过，这只是用户个人的推测。 OpenAI Support 账号随后在帖子下作出回复，表示由于涉及具体账号信息，无法在公开社区论坛处理账号停用申诉。用户应通过封禁通知邮件中的链接提出申诉；如果没有收到邮件，可以通过官方申诉表单或帮助中心联系客服。该回复并未解释该用户账号被封的具体原因。（来源：凤凰网科技） 消息称 Anthropic 拟感恩节前上市 寻求募资至多 1000 亿美元 尽管科技股近期遭遇大幅抛售，人工智能公司 Anthropic 仍在推进首次公开募股（IPO），计划在美国感恩节前上市，寻求融资 800

title: 具身智能，也到了 API 时刻？
summary: 具身智能的 API 时刻意味着部分具身模型已经开始具备跨本体迁移、在一定范围内适应新任务的能力。 作者｜Li Yuan 编辑｜郑玄 具身智能，也到了 API 时刻？ 过去，想知道一个具身模型有多强，往往要看它在发布视频里完成了什么任务。不过，这条线正在松动。 就在近期，一些公司开始把另一种检验方式交到开发者手里：接上你自己的机器人，试着把你的任务做出来。 10 月，Physical Intelligence（PI）开放了模型 API 测试。开发者可以上传自己的机器人数据，在平台上微调模型，再通过云端推理驱动机器人。PI 表示，一家公司，用这套服务迭代了四天，让双臂机器人开始为自身的零部件去毛刺。 同月，Dream Labs 推出 Dream API，将机器人模型推理按作业时长计费，并提供面向开发者数据的模型微调服务。让机器人调用云端模型，正在成为一种可以试用、适配和购买的服务。 国内，11 月 3 日，原力灵机升级了 Dexmal MaaS，将重点放在模型进入具体场景所需的后训练上：开发者可以在同一平台完成数据上传、模型训练和部署，再根据真机执行中的失败继续改进。 这些动作让具身智能行业出现了一个值得关注的变化。过去，我们常常听到一些公司宣称自己在某个场景正在寻求落地突破。而现在，模型公司开始尝试把自己积累的能力，交给不同硬件、不同任务背后的开发者使用。具身模型的竞争，也由此延伸到一个更实际的问题：别人能不能拿它做成应用？ 这一步比语言模型开放 API 要重得多。机器人需要适配自己的身体，理解现场的物体和流程，还要在执行出错时把任务接着做下去。把模型交到外部开发者手里，就意味着让它走出熟悉的实验环境，接受不同本体和真实任务的检验。这需要模型能力作为底气，也需要公司有信心把尚未解决的问题暴露出来，在使用中继续改进。 未来具身智能的形态，或许就会在这些尝试中逐渐清晰。 01 为什么是现在？ 本体厂商提供身体、模型公司提供基础能力，开发者围绕场景构建应用，是行业早已讨论过的一种分工。不过在过往，借助通用模型构建具身应用，仍然往往是一个愿景。 如今，几家公司相继开放 API，开始把这种设想变成开发者可以上手的服务。为什么是现在？ 或许有几点原因。 首先，一部分具身模型开始具备跨本体迁移、在一定范围内适应新任务的能力。 过去，教机器人完成一个新任务，往往意味着围绕特定硬件开发算法、采集数据，再反复调试。具身基础模型正在改变这个起点。模型从不同任务的训练中积累物理世界知识和操作经验，开发者便有机会借用这些能力，把新增投入集中在自己的机器人和任务上。一个基模能够支持的本体与场景越多，将它作为公共服务提供的价值就越大。 PI 展示的一个案例，甚至让机器人参与了自己的制造。开发双臂机器人 Axol 的公司 Almond，希望让它处理自身装配所需的零件。借助 Pi API，这个团队经过四天迭代，让机器人开始为装配用的垫块去毛刺。 原力灵机开放 MaaS，同样有一个能力上的前提：它的基模已经积累了一批能够交给外部开发者使用的操作经验。 按照原力灵机展示的 DM0.5 的 Zero-shot 能力，模型目前已经可以完成抓取、推动、放置、叠放等操作，也能根据颜色、形状和大小区分物体，甚至能完成擦东西这样的更难的操作。 DM 0.5 还能执行序列指令，机器人需要理解多个操作之间的先后关系，完成前一步后，面对已经变化的现场继续执行下一步。DM0.5 对序列指令的支持，加上原生记忆能力，为任务从单个动作延伸到连续操作提供了基础。 这意味着，机器人开始能够把「看懂要求」与「做出动作」连起来：面对不同物体，判断指令指向哪一个，再按要求完成操作。开发者接入之后，已经有一组可以组合、验证的能力，而不必逐项从头训练。 这个起点还需要经得起本体和环境的变化。DM0.5 将多本体适配、原生记忆，以及对光照、相机变化和外界干扰的鲁棒性纳入能力设计。这些特性与开放服务直接相关：外部用户的机器人、工作环境和操作流程各不相同，模型只有能够承接一定程度的变化，共享基础能力才有实际意义。 原力灵机的判断也落在这里。唐文斌此前谈到，一个模型是否好用，要看它能否具备足够强的泛化能力，以及能否通过后训练，省时省力地变成面向具体任务的专用模型。MaaS 将这两种使用方式放在一起：开发者既可以调用通用模型，也可以继续训练适合自身任务的模型。 另一个推动力，来自模型计算需求与机器人身体之间的矛盾。 谈到机器人调用云端模型，人们最先担心的往往是延迟：画面传出去，等模型算完再把动作传回来，会不会已经错过了反应时机？把推理放在端侧，自然是一个直观选择。 但本地部署也未必是最终解法。像 GPT-6 Astra 这样的探索，已经让人看到：持续理解环境、记住交互过程、判断下一步做什么，会对模型提出越来越高的要求。如果机器人也要获得这些能力，本体需要承担的计算负担也会增加，而功耗、散热、续航和成本都会限制算力配置。 云端或现场服务器因此有理由长期参与其中。远程推理能否成立，关键在于如何安排网络传输、模型计算和动作执行。模型可以一次输出一小段动作，机器人执行当前动作时，系统继续计算后续动作，再将两段动作衔接起来。PI 公布的实时动作分块研究，探索的就是如何让模型计算与动作执行重叠，降低推理延迟对连续作业的影响。 原力灵机 MaaS 则将云端模型推理与本地动作执行连接起来：机器人上传相机图像和当前状态，模型预测后续动作，再交由本地控制程序执行。配套的 DexOS Lite 提供推理循环、多步动作执行和请求重试等能力，减少开发者自行衔接这些环节的工作。模型能力向外开放，也需要这样的工程配套，才能落到真实机器人上。 延迟仍然需要处理。网络波动有多大、任务要求多快的反应、动作能否平稳衔接，都会影响远程推理的适用范围。但在一定任务和系统条件下，这些问题已经可以被工程方案容纳。 可复用的基础能力，让开发者有了调用模型的理由；推理与执行方式的改进，让这种调用有机会进入真实作业。具身 API 因而开始具备实际应用的条件。而模型接到客户的机器人之后，能否稳定完成客户的任务，则是下一道更深的门槛。 02 接上模型之后，工作才刚开始 当模型能力和推理条件逐渐成熟，开发者开始有机会借用一个现成的「大脑」。但不同具身 API 能帮用户走多远，差别可能很大。 最基础的影响条件是基础模型的跨本体能力。机械臂的活动范围、夹爪的结构、相机的位置发生变化，模型已有的操作经验能否继续发挥作用，决定了开发者是在已有能力上做适配，还是接近重新教一台机器人干活。 Dream Labs 将跨本体零样本能力作为 Dream-1 的重要卖点。目前，这种能力主要面向双臂平行夹爪机器人，表现也受到本体运动学和控制系统的影响。公司同时提供 FaaS 微调服务，为开发者的机器人定制模型。 在其公布的跨本体仿真评估中，微调提升了多数受测机器人的语言指令跟随得分，但并非所有本体都获得提升。对使用者而言，硬件被列入支持范围之后，仍需要验证模型在自己任务上的效果。 模型适应了新的身体，还要继续适应现场。 比如，把鸡蛋放进蛋托，模型可能已经具备抓取和放置的能力。但鸡蛋滑了一下、蛋托被碰偏，第一次抓取落空后，机器人还能不能调整动作，把任务接着做完？这些情况不一定出现在最初的示范中，却会在实际运行里反复发生。 现阶段，这些问题绕不开后训练。基模提供一个更好的起点，开发者仍然需要用自己的机器人和任务数据，让模型适应现场。如果一项服务只展示接入时的便利，却把此后的适配工作全部留给用户，那么它的 API 服务，并不够真诚。 PI 的 API 因此将数据上传、微调和托管推理连在一起。外部团队采集示范、训练模型、放到机器人上测试，再根据失败决定下一轮补充什么数据。 原力灵机此次 MaaS 升级，也把重点放在了接入之后的适配上。开发者可以上传任务示范进行训练，也可以根据真机运行中的偏差补充纠正数据，进一步利用失败记录优化策略。从学会基本流程，到出错后能够恢复，平台为不同阶段的问题提供了对应的训练路径。 从 PI、Dream Labs 到原力灵机，值得关注的是，它们都把后续适配纳入了服务。即使强调零样本能力，也为效果不够好的情况准备了继续训练的入口。这种安排体现了一种务实：模型能够承担多少，哪些还需要现场数据补足，需要在产品里有明确的位置。 API 的质量，正是在这些后训练的细节里拉开距离。 任务失败之后，「再采一些数据」并不是一个足够有效的建议。开发者需要判断，机器人究竟卡在哪个环节，应该补充什么样的示范，是否需要从出错的状态开始演示恢复过程，以及下一轮测试如何确认问题得到改善。采集什么数据，本身就包含了对任务和模型的理解。 原力灵机就特别关注这一环节，将数据采集指南纳入后训练服务。它的价值在于把现场适配的经验交给开发者，让用户面对失败时，有依据判断下一轮该采什么、怎么采，减少盲目增加数据和反复重训的投入。 围绕数据的后续使用，平台支持上传主流的 LeRobot v3 格式数据集，并通过可视化工作台管理数据和模型、发起定制训练、部署专属模型。从指导采集到训练部署，这些环节连在一起，才能让开发者在现场积累的经验，持续转化为机器人的能力。 03 把后训练交到开发者手里 放在这一轮具身 API 开放潮中看，原力灵机此次 MaaS 升级其实很令人惊喜：既敢于把模型交给外部任务检验，也愿意把开发者接入之后最费力的适配工作，纳入自己的产品责任。 原力灵机是国内较早布局具身 MaaS 的公司。今年 7 月 9 日，它在开发者大会上发布 MaaS 时，就已将云端模型调用、在线后训练和定制模型托管部署纳入服务。 此次升级，则把这条路径进一步细化：从数据采集指南、上传管理，到 SFT 示范学习、DAgger 运行纠偏，再到通过 RECAP 利用失败记录优化策略，平台开始更具体地处理开发者在现场适配中遇到的问题。 业内已经有不少开源模型，但拿到代码之后，怎样准备数据、组织训练、判断效果，再根据失败继续迭代，仍然需要相当的模型经验。国内能把这些后训练工具真正用起来的人，或许只有千人的量级。 而未来可能用上模型服务的团队，能力未必长在这里。本体厂商熟悉硬件，场景团队掌握业务流程，它们需要把这些积累转化为机器人可以执行的任务。数据该怎么采，运行中的偏差怎么纠正，反复出现的失败怎样用于下一轮训练，都需要有具体的方法可以遵循。 把这些方法交到开发者手里，让应用团队不必先成为模型专家，也有办法把任务继续做下去，才是让 MaaS 务实生长的关键。 比如，一支团队想让机器人在传送线侧完成供包。它需要的，是把不同形态、不同摆放状态的包裹持续抓取、放置，并达到现场要求的作业节拍。 通过 MaaS，开发者可以从 DM0.5 已有的操作能力出发，先按照采集指南，用自己的机器人录制任务示范，上传到平台进行 SFT 训练。模型由此学习现场的物体、动作和流程，开发者也不必为这一步自行搭建整套训练系统。 第一版模型部署到机器人上之后，就可以开始检验：哪些包裹能稳定处理，哪些状态容易抓偏，任务又会在哪一步中断。这些结果决定下一轮需要补什么数据。 如果机器人已经能完成基本流程，却经常在执行中发生偏差，开发者可以在它出错时介入，记录如何调整、怎样继续完成任务，再将纠正数据用于 DAgger 训练。下一轮，模型学习的就是这些实际遇到的困难，而不必只靠增加顺利完成的示范碰运气。 对于反复出现的失败，还可以使用 RECAP 继续优化。平台针对任务训练价值模型，为执行记录逐帧生成价值标签，再利用这些评价训练控制机器人动作的策略模型。成功、纠正和失败的记录，都有机会成为改善表现的依据。 这几种方法可以按需选择。每完成一轮训练，开发者就将更新后的模型部署回机器人，检查成功率是否提高、无效尝试是否减少、人工接管是否更少，再决定下一轮的工作。DexOS Lite 或 MaaS API 则负责连接模型服务与机器人，让这套迭代能够落实到真机执行上。 据原力灵机介绍，经过针对具体本体和场景的后训练，平台已在部分真实场景的原子任务测试中实现 100% 成功率。这对应的是特定条件下的单项任务表现，换到新的本体或场景，仍可能需要继续适配。 在物流供包场景，公司披露，使用其 MaaS 的机器人综合作业节拍超过每小时 1200 件，整体成功率超过 99%。平台进一步开放训练与迭代能力，是希望让更多团队也能围绕自己的任务改善效果，并通过作业节拍、人工接管和运行成本，检验应用是否真正算得过账。 除物流供包外，原力灵机披露的应用还包括仓储拆零分拣、手机产线废料回收，手机打包、装配等环节也在持续测试与部署中。 现阶段，具身应用的开发分工仍在形成。能够接入模型的团队，未必同时熟悉生产现场；掌握场景需求的客户，也未必具备模型训练能力。原力灵机一方面通过自身的场景实践处理这些问题，另一方面将训练、部署和本体接入能力向外开放，尝试把更多环节连接起来。 具身智能进入 API 时刻，最终意味着需要由开发者与原力灵机这样的模型公司共同来验证：它们能否借助模型服务做出可用的应用，让机器人持续工作，并算出一笔成立的账。 title: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind <details><summary>
summary: Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work - I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today's coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions. They're too good at describing the work The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That's a lot of information to absorb. It's not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop! It's very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as "I'm not reading all of that". It doesn't matter how accurate or useful the information is, I'm instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me! I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long

title: Terry Pratchett's Study
summary: My comment on Terry Pratchett's Study — Hacker News. Terry Pratchett once wrote about the concept of "horizontal wealth". Vertical wealth is where you spend money on rich people stuff - yachts and suchlike. Horizontal wealth is where you spend more money on the things you liked before you got rich: https://chibuikeani.blogspot.com/2017/02/the-price-of-happin... But horizontal wealth means not letting your increased income dictate your tastes. You like books and now you have money? Buy more books! Change those catenary bookshelves for good hardwood ones! In my case, build a library extension to your office. And, of course, you buy what will be useful for that most wonderful of pursuits, blind research, which is research without direction for the sheer joy of it. (Original source is his book A Slip of the Keyboard - this linked blog post quotes that bit.) Tags: hacker-news , terry-pratchett

Because getting the word out is really important in the early days. Otherwise, you will have no one to try and use your solution. The one thing I struggled with when I was managing a growing team, sales, finances, and projects were that I had to switch between several tools. There was no way to keep everything centralized, so I could save my time and spend more time on growing my business. I talked to other fellow company or agency owners and freelancers who were struggling with the same thing. This is when I decided to start working on a platform where I and other business owners like me will be able to manage everything related to our business in one place. I launched the first and beta version on Agiled in late 2019 and officially launched our product in early 2020. We launched on Betalist and some other startup sites and got some early users. We were soon approached by Appsumo, and In July 2020, we launched on their platform. Our Appsumo launch was a huge boost. We got thousands of new visitors to our website, new users, customers, etc. We have been growing ever since. Take us through the process of designing, prototyping, and manufacturing your first product. We designed our platform with customers in mind. I sat down with the team several times and brainstormed what the customer pain points were. We started with the basic parts of the application like client management, invoicing, estimates, tasks, team managed and evolved our product from there. After our MVP was developed we invited fellow founders and business owners to try the platform and we kept updating our platform based on their feedback until a public beta was ready. Customer feedback is really important when you are developing a software platform. But getting customer feedback can be really difficult. We got thousands of messages with helping feedback and we have been improving our app based on that feedback ever since. One thing we learned while designing a SaaS app is that you have to keep user experience in mind. User experience is the most important part of developing a product. We have improved almost every area of our app. We have released a new small business CRM to help businesses manage their contacts, leads, and prospects in one place. Our project management features have also come a long way to make managing work easy. We also improved other features like contract management , creating proposals , managing team , etc with the help of our users. We also launched some new features like appointing scheduling and meeting booking, subscription management , workflow automations , onboarding flows etc with the help of customer feedback. Our platform was bootstrapped and completely self-funded. We used our Agency income to fund this project. We were able to stay within the budget because we used Agency resources (Devs, Servers, etc) for Agiled. After our Appsumo launch, we expanded our team really quickly to increase the pace of development and to develop new features. Describe the process of launching the business. After our MVP was ready, we reached out to our friends who were business owners and invited them to try out the platform. Of course, we had limited friends so there wasn’t much traction. We built our website and started posting in online communities and started submitting our app in software directories like Betalist, etc. We actually acquired our first few customers from Betalist . After directory submissions users gradually started to come but there wasn’t much volume. We also started working on helpful content to get organic traffic. We built huge template libraries like Invoice Templates , Small Business Resource Hub , Contract Templates , and other helpful content. This content helped us in increasing our visibility in Google and helped us in getting organic users. Sometime after our directory submissions and Betalist launch, we were approached by Appsumo. Our Appsumo launch is what really made the difference in our user base grew exponentially after our launch. Appsumo launch also helped us in cash injection which in turn helped us to grow from a team of 5 to a team of 15+. The Customer is the real boss and customer experience is everything. We keep our customers in the loop on what’s coming next to Agiled and what changes and improvements are we making in our platform. We also email our customers to help them with our product and that has really helped us in retaining our customers. We have also worked on a lot of videos for our Youtube channel which has helped us in attracting new customers. We release a video on every feature launch where I give a quick walk-through of the new feature personally. I’m Nick Nikolaiev and I’m the co-founder of Tactiq. io , a B2C2B (business to consumer to business) productivity SaaS startup. Tactiq is a B2B productivity SaaS browser extension driven by product-led growth - we have a freemium pricing model with paid pro and team accounts. Think Loom or Grammarly, with a similar B2B + B2C distribution, but monetization predominantly through B2B customers. Our main and only product is our Google Chrome/Microsoft Edge browser extension Tactiq.io, which integrates with Google Meet and Zoom. Our application transcribes remote meetings, extracts insights (highlights, keywords), and lets you share them with your team. The product essentially takes notes for you and captures all the crucial meeting outputs whilst you engage in conversation. Product, engineering, sales, and design teams at organizations like Netflix Salesforce are customers. So are micro-agencies, freelancers, and accessibility organizations - we find that effectively anyone who engages in virtual meetings has a use case for Tactiq.io. We’ve grown 20 x Year-on-Year over the last year, and grew from 0 - 150,000+ users in our first year. What s your backstory and how did you come up with the idea? Before Tactiq, I was working on AI products across Europe and the US, with a focus on IT productivity solutions. I came to Australia to complete my MBA at UNSW and founded my previous startup, TaskPace AI, an AI management assistant for Salesforce users. Operating as CEO at TaskPace was what led me to Tactiq. I say this because whilst operating Taskpace as CEO, I lived in Silicon Valley, San Francisco but my engineering team was based in New Zealand. As you can imagine, this meant many remote meetings across time zones. I noticed my team’s meeting productivity was directly correlated to the information captured, shared, and then implemented from our meetings. Put something out there before you feel it’s ready because the only validation that matters is the market. At the same time, my co-founder Ksenia was at Atlassian working on team productivity solutions and saw a similar trend. We both experienced the same problems when it came to remote working environments. We both observed that meeting productivity is highly related to the amount of information captured during the meeting. Meetings are tremendously more productive if the insights aren’t lost or action items are forgotten. Initially, I thought that a transcription tool could be the solution. If you could record and document meeting discussions to ensure no action items or essential insights were forgotten, that would solve the problem. But as we worked through this solution, we realized that real-time transcription only scrapes the surface of the problem with remote meeting productivity. Beyond capturing critical information, I recognized that teams need to be able to extract all the important details and insights from meetings, then push that data into Calendars, CRMs, Customer databases, slack channels, etc for it to have an impact. The problem space expanded with an epiphany that it wasn’t just about documentation but making meeting outcomes seamless. Take us through the process of designing, prototyping, and manufacturing your first product. I would say our process followed the lean-startup method very closely. First, we defined the problem space, as “not capturing important information and insights during meetings creates unproductivity and wastes time when meeting action items aren’t implemented or important insights are lost”. Next, we looked for the simplest possible solution to the problem. We landed on real-time transcription of meetings to document the conversation, action items, and insights for implementation. However, this posed a serious challenge - real-time transcription of audio requires a powerful AI engine for voice-to-text interpretation. For context, the only competent voice-to-text engines are created by the likes of Apple (Siri), Baidu, and Google, companies with billions in R D to throw at training their AI/ML algorithms. So we sort of stumbled on a solution - to build on voice-to-text infrastructure created by google in Google Meets (closed-captioning). In hindsight, I think this was a smart decision, as we drastically reduced development time and costs by building on this infrastructure. It’s a lesson I’d like to impart to other founders - if there’s a way to build your MVP on an existing foundation/infrastructure, do it. You will drastically de-risk the development process and increase your speed to validation. My co-founder Ksenia mocked up some wireframes of the UI and product interface in Figma, and together we agreed on the critical functionality we’d need to validate the product. Ksenia Svechnikova - any inputs around your process for this? how you : designed the Tactiq services/offerings, designed the initial features, the early user interfaces, MVP, etc Describe the process of launching the business. We launched our MVP on the Google Chrome store in March of 2020. On launch day my co-founder and I promoted our launch to all our socials, then shared the link to a few other channels (Reddit, quora, etc). Over the next few months, my co-founder Ksenia spent hours each day sharing a link to our extension everywhere people were asking for this solution online - Reddit, Twitter, Quora, youtube, you name it. Within the first 3 months, we had our first 10,000 users. There are three factors I attribute to our early traction. One - product-market fit and a real need for our service, evidenced by hundreds of quora/Reddit/Twitter threads about the problem (transcribing google meets). This made it easy to acquire initial users, as we were solving a problem for users who were already seeking a solution. Solving a problem people already experience is much easier than one they don’t understand yet. For other founders, I believe it’s worthwhile gauging market demand by searching for people asking for a solution on Reddit, Twitter, Quora, and other similar channels as a way to pre-validate your solution. The second factor was the timing of the pandemic which caused remote work, online classes, and virtual meetings to explode. And the third was tenacity. The volume of comments, replies, and output from my co-founder and me to promote Tactiq with zero dollars in marketing. We must have published over a thousand replies in those first few months. To finance the business, our initial inputs were only time. We bootstrapped the MVP, with my co-founder building, designing, and launching the product, then together we worked on marketing to free channels. So it was almost zero cost outside of our hours and paying for a few tools. One such tool was Webflow to build our website, Tactiq.io (screenshot of the initial website below). Since launch, what has worked to attract and retain customers? One of the most effective tactics for our growth has been sponsoring Tiktok creators. Our strategy was covered in depth by IndieHackers and DemandCurve. With TikTok, we were able to acquire ~150,000+ new users for our extension by spending USD 1820 working with creators. Over a few months between Oct 2020 and Feb 21, we reached out to creators via Instagram and email to create 22 sponsored TikToks posts. These videos generated 7,363,561 TikTok impressions, 920,426 likes on TikTok, and over 150,000 new users (our tracking wasn t 100% accurate). We even had a few sponsored posts that went viral, generating millions of views, 10-20x spikes in website traffic, and leading to tens of thousands in new sign-ups. Organic Tiktok content is a viral channel, and we capitalized on this by working with talented creators to produce content. It was started in 2021 and ended in 2023. Reason for closure: Shut down. Hello! Who are you and what business did you start? Site Alert was acquired by the team at Southport Ventures in April 2021. Although we are not the founders, we have found a good home for this great product. We purchased the product from Frank Corso, a dedicated and vigilant developer that wanted it to end up in good hands. We liked the metrics, the customer base, and the quality of the codebase. This was an easy deal to love, and the business has only grown since we purchased it. Southport Ventures is an acquisition fund focused on profitable, mission-critical, B2B SaaS businesses. Nicholas Evans and Trevor Ewen founded Southport Ventures in early 2021 to acquire great bootstrapped products in the space. Nicholas has a strong product management background. Trevor is a software engineer. Site Alert is a lightweight monitoring tool targeted at small business owners in charge of 1-50 normal websites. The pricing is very favorable for a non-technical business owner to receive easy monitoring without going down the rabbit hole of IT monitoring, in a much more complicated sense. Critically, the project notifies for downtime, checks for broken links, checks for broken images, and does page performance analysis. All this is within one simple interface with a plug-and-play model. Since our April 2021 acquisition, we’ve continued to run it well over 50% net profit margin while also growing it 51%. How did you find the business and what made you think it’d be a good acquisition? We met the founder via a conference and networking group called MicroAcquire. Given the nature of the community, it is common for founders to sell products. We were particularly interested in this one, because of the reasonable terms relative to the customer list and quality of the code. “Set it and forget it” is thrown around a lot, but that is the case with this product. It allows us to focus our initiatives on growth moves and not get caught up trying to improve an already great customer experience. The founder had run the business as a successful hobby project for several years prior. He was an incredibly skilled developer and very active in the WordPress community. As a result, he had a great deal of organic growth through the WordPress plugin marketplace. His reasons for exit were not financial, he just wanted his time back for other initiatives. This was the basis for our favorable terms because it’s much easier to provide a great exit for a seller if they have goals other than money, particularly if you (the buyer) can serve those goals. Goals: Quick transaction, asset sale, fair price, and customers will no longer reach out to the seller. In other words, we’ll respect his desire to get out of the business. Describe the process of launching the business. When we acquired SiteAlert, we immediately recognized the brand needed a facelift. We launched a brand new, modernized design. Nicholas Evans headed up this process. Since he comes from a design and UX background, he made quick work with a theme we purchased. Before: After: In addition, we had an existing business doing software development ( Southport Technology Group ). We were able to onboard existing clients to the platform and “Eat our dog food” as the industry term goes. Nothing is truly automatic, but it’s hard to beat good organic growth with real creators and business people that rely on a useful service. From there, it’s been smooth sailing finding new avenues of promotion and getting the platform out to business owners that want an alerting system full-featured and cheaper than something like Uptime Robot. Since launch, what has worked to attract and retain customers? Good customer service is a must. The product is very user-friendly, so we have little inbound for customer service. When we do, we have the time and energy to make it happen (because it’s such a small fraction). Beyond that, we are responsive to feature requests. We are currently in the midst of a marketing campaign to increase exposure and let small business owners know there is an all-in-one solution for site monitoring, broken link checking, broken image tests, and more. Our top channel remains as such, and it’s one we accidentally walked into via the acquisition. The product sits on top of a free plugin in the WordPress plugin directory. The network effects in the WordPress marketplace have provided a steady stream of customers and contributed primarily to our existing growth metrics. In addition, we have added Google PPC to increase acquisitions outside of the WordPress marketplace. The goal is to increase conversions for non-WordPress-based hosts because we bear some risk in our centralization on that platform. Still, the WordPress channel endures as our strongest. PPC is a tough game, and something we have put in place mostly as an alternative, but not something we expect to spend a lot of time on. How are you doing today and what does the future look like? The product has done well. 2021 has been a great time for new business upstarts and enhanced web and eCommerce needs for business. Monitoring and peace of mind is critical part of that journey. We are just happy to offer the easiest solution for solo and small entrepreneurs. The free WordPress plugin has 285 5-star reviews and over 239K all-time downloads. The plugin continues to get numerous downloads every month and regular positive reviews. We ve grown revenue 51% since buying it in April 2021 through a combination of experimenting with pricing and paid to advertise. We’ve also maintained a net profit margin of well over 50%. In 2022, we’ll experiment with some newsletters and other forms of paid advertising. We may hire a content creator to write more articles for the blog as well. Our goal is to continue to grow revenue by 50% per year while maintaining high-profit margins. Through starting the business, have you learned anything particularly helpful or advantageous? I will answer the question from the perspective of acquisition. Nothing is truly automatic, but it’s hard to beat good organic growth with real creators and business people that rely on a useful service. What platform/tools do you use for your business? Amazon Lightsail has been an amazing and affordable deployment platform. The services are written in Flask (Python framework). It is very friendly, and we have enjoyed working with it. We use WordPress for our marketing site and blog so we can use our plugin on our site (it’s always good to dog food your products). We use Stripe for payments, ProfitWell for revenue/churn insights, fullstory for funnel analytics, and ConvertKit for marketing email sequences. What have been the most influential books, podcasts, or other resources? Podcasts: Startups for the Rest of Us , Businessology , Side Hustle Show (Nick Loper) . Advice for other entrepreneurs who want to get started or are just starting out? The acquisition is a great way to get started. If you don’t have an idea, you can always unload one (or many) from others trying to move on. Where can we go to learn more? If you're interested in reading how they got started, published about 7 years ago, check it out here. Hello again! Remind us who you are and what business you started. Hello, my name is Mitchell and it’s good to be back. I am the Director of Administration (self-appointed title) of Patriot Chimney , which means I am over marketing, accounting, customer service, and all things on the “business” side of it. We are a full-service chimney company, but also provide dryer vent maintenance and repair. In 2021, we have 3 vans and 5 full-time employees serving our customers every day. We’re set to cross $500,000 for the first time this year. We haven’t finished closing the books for November, so through October, we’ve earned $463,000, which is 30.81% more than last year. Tell us about what you’ve been up to! Has the business been growing? The business has been growing! We’re up about 30% since last year, and we’re looking for ways that we can increase business. The problem isn’t so much how to get leads, but rather how to service them fast enough. We’re actively hiring new technicians, but we can’t train them fast enough to get them out in the field for meaningful work beyond training. We’re booking more than 60 days out and considering NOT taking new customers for the rest of the year and a couple of months next year. This is a very scary option, but we’ll likely need to go this route to help slow things down. The obvious solution would likely be to raise our prices. We did that, We raised our inspections from $85 to $250 per inspection. The goal was to limit the number of new customers (all repair jobs start with an inspection) we’d take on. To also help, we’ve constricted our service area by only servicing about a 30-mile radius around Roanoke, VA, where we’re located. We’re doing all of this in the hope that we can get to our customers a lot faster than 60 days. Our ultimate goal going into 2022 is to get to customers within 14 days on average. The most impactful project we completed was the implementation of the Entrepreneur Operating System (EOS) which is a decision-making framework to help get your business to the next level. We created core values, 1-year goals, 3-year goals, and a big goal. All of our decision-making is based around these items and helping us achieve the goals while also falling within our core values. Without EOS or some other framework and goals, you’re trying to put together a puzzle without looking at the box. There’s no vision; no guideline for your business to grow into. Now we have that, and I can tell that there’s a big focus on achieving our goals. What have been your biggest lessons learned in the last year? Give yourself room to fail. You’ve probably heard about allowing yourself to fail. You should do that too. Without taking risks, you’re limiting your creativity, innovation, and risk. But I’m talking about giving yourself room to fail. This means giving a buffer so that if things go wrong (they will) you won’t be scrambling around trying to move things around. Think of it as going to the airport. It’s recommended that you arrive two hours before boarding. This gives you enough time to check your bags, go through TSA (even with extra checks from them), get a snack, use the bathroom, and still relax before boarding. By getting there early, you’re giving yourself room for a buffer in case things go wrong. In our business, as I mentioned before, we’re booked solid for the next couple of months. We work outside, so we rely on dry weather for safe access to the customer’s roofs. If it rains and we can’t do the work, we need to reschedule. The problem is when we have to schedule this customer, we have a list of other customers that we’ll also need to reschedule and we’re in a bit of a domino effect trying to get to our customers fast enough and not messing up the schedule too bad. If we give ourselves room to fail, by maybe keeping a day open each week or only scheduling new jobs for the first half of the day, we’d be able to adjust a lot easier by filling the open days and time slots. What’s in the plans for the upcoming year, and the next 5 years? Our 1-year goal is to reach $800,000 in revenue with 10% profit and have 10 total employees with four work vans. We’ll decrease the time it takes to get to our customers to an average of 14 days. We’ll also implement a much better training program that will allow employees to go from trainee to technician much faster. We’re entrepreneurs and we want to solve problems, but focus on one at a time. We don’t have a set 5-year goal with EOS, but we do have a three-year goal. By then, we’ll be at $1.5 million in revenue and $150,000 in profit. We’ll have 17 total employees and 6 work vans. We’ll also move into a much larger office/warehouse. Have you read any good books in the last year? The number one book I read was Traction . This lays out everything you need to know about EOS and how you can implement it in your business. I’ve also read the HBR guide to Buying a Small Business . I also own another business, Town Mountain Maids , and growth through acquisition is a huge growth strategy we’re focusing on right now. This book helps layout how to buy a business even if you don’t have a ton of upfront capital. Advice for other entrepreneurs who might be struggling to grow their business? Stay focused. I can’t stress this enough. Too many entrepreneurs get started and have this idea for a huge holding company, Warren Buffet style, and it causes them to lose focus on the tasks at hand. It’s so easy to get distracted. We’re entrepreneurs and we want to solve problems but focus on one at a time. I have two businesses and I focus on both. But there are ebbs and flows where I’m working on Patriot Chimney a lot more than Town Mountain Maids. And then I’ll work on a project for Town Mountain Maids and put Patriot Chimney on the back burner. I’m able to do this because I took the time up front to focus on these businesses and built a team of support (when we had enough revenue) that can handle a lot while I’m on the next project for a different company. If you're interested in reading how they got started, published almost 6 years ago, check it out here. Hello again! Remind us who you are and what business you started. I m the CEO of Soundbrenner . Our goal is to design the world s best music tools to make music practice addictive. We serve musicians of all instruments and skill levels. We make a range of wearables that help you play on the beat, stay in tune, protect your hearing, and more. To date, we shipped over 100,000 wearables. Besides this, we also make a mobile app for iOS Android that is free but also comes with a subscription. To date, we have over 8M downloads and over 670,000 monthly active users. Tell us about what you’ve been up to! Has the business been growing? Since last year the most exciting addition to the business has been a subscription service for our mobile app. Since we had such a huge user base, we wanted to hire additional mobile app engineers and invest in developing additional features. Now that the app provides a sustainable revenue channel we can do this. Always run towards your fear, and you ll be unstoppable. Being in the consumer electronics business is tough because R D is very expensive, takes very long, requires a lot of capital, and on top is also seasonal. By unlocking a second revenue channel for the business we can now offset some of these challenges. Also, I m a strong believer in the narrative that making your hardware allows you to create the best experiences. So now we can truly integrate software + hardware and create something magical we couldn t otherwise do for our customers. What have been your biggest lessons learned in the last year? A lesson we learned this year specifically for e-commerce was to add 3rd party brands to our website. Up until today, we could only sell a customer a single product and we would be done at least for a couple of years until we released a new generation because there was just no reason to buy another one of our devices. However, we had so many website visitors (100k+ / month) as well as a huge email list (200k+). All these people loved and trusted our brand, we re interested potential buyers of music equipment but we had nothing to sell them. So we tried out adding some 3rd party products and this worked like wonder and way better than we could have ever hoped! 3rd party products now represent over 33% of our monthly revenue. We also started offering protection plans for sale and expanded our accessories (screen protectors, etc.). All this adds up and allows you to up your digital marketing budgets since the return on ad spend naturally goes up. What’s in the plans for the upcoming year, and the next 5 years? We are right now looking at the crypto space because we feel like there are some really exciting opportunities for musicians in the future. Besides this, of course, we plan to launch tons of new features for our apps, including a completely new category (practice tracking practice motivation). We also have some updates for our hardware in-store, so all around, I m excited for what s to come. I still feel like we only have reached 1% of our potential and are still at the start of our journey. This feels somewhat crazy to say after 7 years but you don t change the world overnight! Have you read any good books in the last year? My favorite thinker I started following the last 12 months is probably Balaji . If you haven t, you should check out his appearance on the Tim Ferris podcast . In line with this, I love the Praxis Society project and want to give it a shoutout. I m excited to see communities forming that celebrate progress achievement, and dream big in the physical world. It feels like the smartest people were all wandering exclusively in the digital world for the past 20 years but that is changing. I m stoked! Besides this, I m re-reading Fountainhead at the moment and would highly recommend checking it out. Advice for other entrepreneurs who might be struggling to grow their business? It s really hard to give broad advice since lack of growth could have so many different reasons. It might be due to poor marketing, a too-small market, a poor product market fit, etc. When faced with really hard challenges I often found I already knew what the problem was, but was avoiding dealing with it. There s a great article from Ben Horowitz about this. Do you run towards your fear or do you run away from it? So my advice: always run towards your fear, and you ll be unstoppable. If you're interested in reading how they got started, published almost 6 years ago, check it out here. Hello again! Remind us who you are and what business you started. I m Jonathan Bradford, founder of The Hygeine Company , a business started through personal experience. In 1976, I eft school with what I considered to be very little education or indeed O / A levels results to say I was a bright lad capable of learning. Interestingly enough my parents never asked to see my results. I can’t honestly say I liked school, why would I, I found it difficult nothing seemed to sink in and stay there. In leaving School I did, however, sign on for college which I did enjoy but unfortunately it only lasted 1 year – the second year closed down after two weeks due to a lack of attendees. Out to work helping out on a large 4 colour industrial printer ( I was just the young lad feeding paper into one end , whereby it would go through the print rollers and come out the other end looking lovely, from memory this last 12-18 months Then on to work at my Dad s engineering factory whereby I went through all different aspects of production, using CNC punching machines to welding to preparing metal pre-painting to paint to assembly and packaging. Not realising at the time just how much work experience meant to me. For 12 years my elder brother, sister and myself Imported promoted and distributed Windsurfing and snow skiing / boarding equipment, this was not only fantastic fun, a job which I never really saw as a job but more a case of having fun whilst at the same time making a good living - little was I to know the experience and knowledge I was gaining would help set me up for life. 1992 after 12 fantastic years we lost a major windsurfing brand agency which in turn meant I was now out of work. In 1992 having found myself unemployed I decided to join the local Health Fitness club. Playing lots of Squash Racketball going into the gym - soon recognized an opening for antibacterial wipes in Health Fitness to wipe down equipment after use .. then started our journey. Tell us about what you’ve been up to! Has the business been growing? How did we react to the demands of the pandemic? 2020 Covid hits – demands for product goes through the roof to the extent we must implement a NO new customers policy simply look after and service existing customers only. Demand was such that we and to commission the services of 6 additional suppliers from around the world to try and meet the demands of our customers. In order to meet demands, in addition to our UK supply’s we soon found ourselves in a position whereby we had 20 x forty containers on route from the Far East , in between the orders being placed, shipped and arrival (usually 12 weeks’ time scale) we suddenly found ourselves in a position whereby the country is in lockdown , everybody is canceling orders due to the fact businesses were shut and we had nowhere near enough storage space, panic sets in. By the end of our financial year in 2020 – 2021 whereas we were on target to hit £6m - due to lockdown we ended up at £3.7M not bad considering pre-Covid we were at £1.5m, the point here being it shows just how well we as a company reacted, the team pulled together and worked what felt like 24/7 to meet customer demands. Frantically searching the UK for additional storage, we were lucky enough to find local storage in a clean dry warehouse within 6 miles of our offices. February 2021 and we have in the region of 500 pallets stacked high and waiting for businesses to re-open, by late 2021 we are getting through the stock and placing orders for more production. 2022 we’re off to a flying start business is plentiful, yet how long we can continue at this pace is to be seen. It has been a full-on past 24 months without a break. We have had to take on additional staff and production throughout this pandemic. I feel it would be a mistake to assume business will remain at this rate as has been proven time and time again. People soon become complacent, lazy, forgetful, or simply can’t be bothered. After all, It is was nearly 200 years since Ignaz Semmelweis recognised the importance of washing ones hands – it seems to take a pandemic for us to appreciate the importance of clean hands and clean surfaces. 2020 -2021 end of the financial at £3.7m 2021 – 2022, We look to be on target for £2.6m, yes down on 2020 – 2021 but that’s to be expected given as a country we have experienced lockdown on several occasions with businesses closed, people working from home, offices at low occupancy. It’s a new world out there, all businesses have had to adapt and re-evaluate how they operate, we can but hope people have learned the importance of clean hands and clean surfaces. As a final thought! Whereas the best form of cleaning one s hands is undoubtedly soap and water and correct drying procedure, for this kills, removes, and washes dead bacteria down the sink, whereas antibacterial gels may kill germs and bacteria, this dead bacteria remains on your hands, yet an antibacterial wipe not only kills but it also REMOVES germs bacteria. We specialize in antibacterial wipes dispensers, antibacterial wipes, hand sanitizers, and monitors which record compliance to cleaning procedures and report any issues of concern in real-time. Unlike many that jumped on the bandwagon throughout the pandemic, this has been our business for 30 years. We supply product around the world, with our products being found in locations such as The US Embassy In London The Houses of Parliament, P O cruise liners, Oslo Airport, Schools Universities, Offices Health Fitness, shopping centres, in fact just about anywhere, where compliance to good hand surface hygiene is recognised as important . The next 12/24 months – watch this space we continue to Innovate Design Manufacture. What have been your biggest lessons learned in the last year? Stick to what you know - there have been so many companies from so many different industries jumping on the bandwagon to try and capitalize on a Pandemic . So many getting their hands burnt ending up with thousands of pounds worth of stock which they simply cannot move due to excess supply in the market. Know when to stop throwing money at a project that just isn’t going to work. What’s in the plans for the upcoming year, and the next 5 years? Compliance with good hand surface Hygiene practices will be improved and adhered to if you make it convenient for the user, our motto has always been “within arms reach” We look adapt and improve our desktop / surface mounted dispensers in order that our WIPEPOD becomes part of your office / school / working desk. We look to continue to promote and develop our Biodegradable range. Here s one for you that you won’t have seen before and we are once again we are the first - antibacterial wipes from a box, yes just as you get your milk and even wine in a box, why not Antibacterial wipes to try and replace the plastic bucket. Have you read any good books in the last year? I love reading especially autobiographies but pretty much only on holiday, given the pandemic I haven’t traveled for 2 years. Advice for other entrepreneurs who might be struggling to grow their business? For most, we included, its time and effort and hard work - keep adding the FUEL (time Effort) knock on doors - Online - Social media, exhibitions meet the buyer s events - but as the Dragons will so often tell you - know when to stop throwing money at a project that just isn’t going to work. Take us through the process of designing, prototyping, and manufacturing your first product. Setting up the manufacturing of the smart glasses was one of the hardest obstacles that we faced as we had to find a partner that had experience developing cutting edge electronics especially in the AR space. There were only a few manufacturers in this space and almost all of them worked exclusively with public companies. We found an excellent manufacturing partner who picked us because of our extensive experience, our strong customer base, and the unique advantages of our product, like a smaller size, android based, etc. when compared to the competition. We designed our smart glasses in a scaleable, manufacturable way- meaning that we did not use too many custom components except for our IP. How I Started A $48K/Month Business With An Online Fitness Training Service (2019) ➜ This is a follow up story for TeamFFLEX. If you're interested in reading how they got started, published almost 7 years ago, check it out here. Hello again! Remind us who you are and what business you started. My name is Ryan Milton and I am the owner and founder of TeamFFLEX . We coach professional athletes, Npc and Ifbb competitors, Hollywood actors, professional musicians, and everyday people all around the world. Since we last spoke my business is now breaking a million a year. Tell us about what you’ve been up to! Has the business been growing? Since we last spoke, TeamFFLEX has continued to grow and expand. We now have more coaches on the team and many more clients. Month after month, we have continued to grow and expand leading us to right now (literally as I write this) finishing our best month financially of all time. I don’t have any new fancy tips or tricks that will be your “cheat sheet” to success. But what I can tell you is that “laying the bricks” has been the biggest way for TeamFFLEX continued growth. The last time we talked, I spoke heavily on how the content was our flagship to generate new business and new leads and nothing has changed. Today even now I spend the bulk of my time delivering our service to our clients and otherwise creating content for free that will help anyone who sees it. Another big contributing factor to where we are now was adding more coaches to the team to help with client load and further delegating much of my day-to-day processes to staff that can accomplish near identical results. The system that I built single-handedly in the beginning now can operate much of the day-to-day without my direct involvement which allows me to spend more time being a better coach and creating better content and that’s huge. In our 1st conversation, I did mention how I did not rely heavily on paid advertising and marketing to get new business and continue to grow and that is still today the truth. I have yet to make any serious efforts at creating ad campaigns and marketing to generate leads. The best marketing for this industry I do still believe is word of mouth and being known for the quality of services offered. Anyone can pump some money behind some ads that make people buy. But I constantly ask myself instead of finding a way to get more leads specifically, how do I improve the quality of the services we offer? By improving the quality of services offered and finding out how to do even more for the customer will always lead to more leads, more customers, and then also a better experience for all current and new customers. Literally unplug. Turn off the news, Turn off the social media, reset your mind and get back to work. When times get tough, work harder. When you get worried, work harder. When you doubt yourself or the state of everything else, work harder. One thing interestingly enough I have now been working to do now is: reduce the amount of content we do, but improve the quality. Initially, as I was growing and scaling my business the content was absolutely key and critical to get the name out there and let the world know what we were about. I used to do youtube videos every day, podcasts every day, social media posts on all platforms every day, live streams, interviews, and whatever else I could do to get the brand out there. The content became creating content for content creation purposes which overtime I felt I was giving less than my best on. When I started to realize this was happening I immediately decided then to scale back the amount of content I was doing overall and instead make a strong effort to make every single piece of content done to serve a deeper and more specific purpose. This meant better actual pieces of content themselves but also more in-depth captions and just overall better for the viewer. I think it is really key when creating content to keep in mind your audience all the time. What do they want to see? What do they want to hear? What can you do to provide that value to them. It is easy to get lost in content creation by just doing what you may want to do or what you may want to see. But if you don’t keep in constant perspective what the person digestion the content will see then you content will never be as good as it could be. What have been your biggest lessons learned in the last year? In the past year, it would be hard to say that the pandemic and everything surrounding it has not been a huge obstacle for every business in the world. Fortunately for us, we have been doing online training for years and years before any of this happened which still allowed us to deliver our services without issue. We did still however have to pivot our focus to more home-style workouts as gyms closed and also continue to develop and create new programs and products that our clients and customers around the world could use to continue to grow. One of the biggest lessons I ve learned throughout the last year has been that you should always be aiming to review and improve whatever it is that you do in your business. Review what you personally do, what your employees do, what your business offers, what services and products you offer, everything. Then decide if it could be better. And if it can be, aim to create that. I have done this countless times since the start of my company and I just recently yet again did this review and changed for the better many things and even added services I wanted to offer in the beginning but didn’t have the ability to support at the time. Every time I take time to review what the day-to-day is and if our systems can be improved I come up with something that improves not only the function of the business but also the function of the employees, the client experience and that just makes everything better for everyone. Never be afraid of change. Never be afraid to make changes and experiment to see what could potentially be even better. Another thing I do want to mention that I think is a super valuable skill to have or learn is the ability to have super discipline to get your work done through all the noise that happens in the world. We live in a crazy world these days where there are so many things that can derail your progress or distract you from focusing on your day-to-day. It s important to remember that losing focus on your business and your customers even for a short time will have lasting effects. If you find yourself getting distracted, if you find yourself losing your discipline to do your work - unplug. Literally unplug. Turn off the news, Turn off the social media, reset your mind and get back to work. When times get tough, work harder. When you get worried, work harder. When you doubt yourself or the state of everything else, work harder. All the hard times and things you could be worried about will eventually end. If you're interested in reading how they got started, published almost 8 years ago, check it out here. Hello again! Remind us who you are and what business you started. Hi guys! My name is Jimmy Cowe and I started Crimibox in 2017. With Crimibox, we make and sell fictional murder cases as an escape game via our webshop. People order their cases online and receive a box full of evidence, pictures, and police files. Together with their online partner, they need to sort out who the murderer is. The idea of selling fictional murder cases started with a post-it on my fridge. I have worked for the police for 12 years so I have seen some incredible stories. I was tired of working for someone and I wanted to start a new business. So I quit, hung a post-it on my fridge to brainstorm for ideas and Crimibox was born! Anno 2021 we are with six full-time employees, had a partnership with a Netflix series, and ended 2020 with 1.5 million as a turnover. We’re also active in more than four languages in twelve countries. More than a quarter of a million worldwide! Tell us about what you’ve been up to! Has the business been growing? It has been crazy times. When COVID hit Belgium in 2020, everything went on lockdown. We couldn’t even go outside if it was unnecessary . People were inside a lot so Crimibox seemed the perfect pastime with your family. For Crimibox, it was a fantastic year. We broke every record there was until April 2021. Everything started to open again and normal life started. Don’t rely on one channel but spread your chances. People could go outside again and they didn’t want to play a game inside. So we knew a decline in our revenue. Q2 and Q3 were not that good but now Q4 is looking good so far. Christmas season and Black Friday are favorable to us. During that time, we hired two new people on our team. From now on, we have our graphic designer which is good for the quality of our boxes and online marketing. We also hired an office manager because a bigger team means a bigger need for structure. Especially when you work with some creative, chaotic minds. There have been a few more obstacles to our business. For example the start of IOS 14. This had a big influence on our marketing strategy. Facebook was until then our number one source of income via online advertising. From now on, we can’t track the outcome precisely anymore so we had to look for other channels. It challenged us to be more creative so we started working more with Google Ads and discovered TikTok Ads as well. 2020 was the first time we participated in the Black Friday madness. Before that, we didn’t believe that this hype would be such a big thing in Europe (as we don’t have Thanksgiving). But we gave it a try and it turned out to be our most successful weekend ever! We hit a conversion rate of 8% which is crazy. What have been your biggest lessons learned in the last year? As I already mentioned, we have had some trouble with the IOS 14 update. Before the update, we almost only relied on Facebook for online advertising. Our advice; don’t rely on one channel but spread your chances. It’s cliché but we experienced it firsthand. Look for new and innovative channels. Try, fail and try again until you find a new channel that works well for your business. For example TikTok, it’s not about Gen Z and dancing anymore. Also, don’t underestimate the power of e-mailmarketing. One of the biggest marketing lessons I learned after four years is that your existing clients are so much more important than acquiring new clients. Keep your existing clients engaged, make them happy, and make them talk about your brand. E-mailmarketing is the ideal tool for that. What’s in the plans for the upcoming year, and the next 5 years? We have some big things ahead for Crimibox. We want to be the biggest in crime entertainment. A big extension of our product range as long as it’s related to crime. Recently we released our first book but there are other things on our planning. A physical experience, a podcast, a subscription model, and if we can dream big, we have our crime streaming service, a crime theme park. We want to focus on true crime fanatics because we believe that that’s a really interesting target audience. If they’re done doing something crime-related, we want them to come to our website to look for the next thing. At this point, we’re working hard behind the scene for a rebranding.
